{{Short description|Model of the Universe proposed 1932}}
The '''Einstein–de Sitter universe''' is a model of the universe proposed by [[Albert Einstein]] and [[Willem de Sitter]] in 1932.<ref>{{cite journal
| author1 = Einstein
| author2 = and De Sitter
| date = 1932
| title = On the relation between the expansion and the mean density of the universe
| journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
| volume = 18
| issue = 3
| pages = 213–214
| doi = 10.1073/pnas.18.3.213 
| bibcode = 1932PNAS...18..213E
| pmc = 1076193
| pmid=16587663
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> On first learning of [[Edwin Hubble]]'s discovery of a linear relation between the redshift of the galaxies and their distance,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hubble|first1=Edwin|title=A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=1929|volume=15|issue=3|pages=168–173|doi=10.1073/pnas.15.3.168|pmid=16577160|pmc=522427|bibcode=1929PNAS...15..168H|doi-access=free}}</ref> Einstein set the [[cosmological constant]] to zero in the [[Friedmann equations]], resulting in a model of the expanding universe known as the [[Friedmann–Einstein universe]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Einstein|first1=Albert|title=Zum kosmologischen Problem der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie|journal=Sitzungs.König. Preuss. Akad.|date=1931|pages=235–237}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=O'Raifeartaigh|first1=and McCann|title=Einstein's cosmic model of 1931 revisited|journal=Eur. Phys. J. H|date=2014|volume=39|issue=1|pages=63–86|doi=10.1140/epjh/e2013-40038-x|arxiv=1312.2192|bibcode=2014EPJH...39...63O|s2cid=53419239}}[https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.2192 Physics ArXiv preprint]</ref> In 1932, Einstein and De Sitter proposed an even simpler cosmic model by assuming a vanishing [[spatial curvature]] as well as a vanishing cosmological constant. In modern parlance, the Einstein–de Sitter universe can be described as a [[Physical cosmology|cosmological]] model for a flat matter-only [[Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric]] (FLRW) universe.<ref name="Bergström & Goobar">[[Lars Bergström (physicist)|Lars Bergström]] & [[Ariel Goobar]]: "''Cosmology and Particle Astrophysics''", 2nd ed. [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] (2004), p. 70+77. {{ISBN|3-540-43128-4}}.</ref><ref name=KahnKahn1975>{{cite journal|last1=Kahn|first1=Carla|last2=Kahn|first2=Franz|author-link2=Franz Daniel Kahn|title=Letters from Einstein to de Sitter on the nature of the Universe|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=257|issue=5526|year=1975|pages=451–454|issn=0028-0836|doi=10.1038/257451a0|bibcode=1975Natur.257..451K|s2cid=4163892}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Einstein|first1=Albert|last2=De Sitter|first2=Willem|date=1932|title=On the Relation between the Expansion and the Mean Density of the Universe|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=18|issue=3|pages=213–214|issn=0027-8424|pmc=1076193|pmid=16587663|bibcode=1932PNAS...18..213E|doi=10.1073/pnas.18.3.213|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In the model, Einstein and de Sitter derived a simple relation between the average density of matter in the universe and its expansion according to ''H''<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> = ''кρ''/3,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=O’Raifeartaigh |first=Cormac |last2=O’Keeffe |first2=Michael |last3=Mitton |first3=Simon |date=2021-03-19 |title=Historical and philosophical reflections on the Einstein-de Sitter model |url=https://doi.org/10.1140/epjh/s13129-021-00007-8 |journal=The European Physical Journal H |language=en |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=4 |doi=10.1140/epjh/s13129-021-00007-8 |issn=2102-6467|arxiv=2008.13501 }}</ref> where ''H''<sub>0</sub> is the [[Hubble constant]], ''ρ'' is the average density of matter and ''к'' is the [[Einstein gravitational constant]]. The size of the Einstein–de Sitter universe evolves with time as <math>a\propto t^{2/3}</math>, making its current age 2/3 times the [[Hubble time]]. The Einstein–de Sitter universe became a standard model of the universe for many years because of its simplicity and because of a lack of empirical evidence for either spatial curvature or a cosmological constant.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Kragh|first1=Helge|title=Cosmology and Controversy|url=https://archive.org/details/cosmologycontrov00helg|url-access=registration|date=1999|publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]|location=New Jersey|page=[https://archive.org/details/cosmologycontrov00helg/page/35 35]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Nussbaumer|first1=Harry|title=Discovering the Expanding Universe|date=2009|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|location=Cambridge|pages=144–152}}</ref>  It also represented an important theoretical case of a universe of critical matter density poised just at the limit of eventually contracting. However, Einstein's later reviews of cosmology make it clear that he saw the model as only one of several possibilities for the expanding universe.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Einstein|first1=Albert|title=The Meaning of Relativity|date=1945|publisher=[[Routledge]]|location=New York|pages=112–135|edition=2nd}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Einstein|first1=Albert|title=La Theorie de la Relativité|date=1933|publisher=Hermann et Cie|location=Paris|pages=99–109}}</ref><ref name="cor-2013">{{cite journal | last1 = O'Raifeartaigh | first1 = O'Keeffe | last2 = Nahm | last3 = Mitton | year = 2015 | title = 'Einstein's cosmology review of 1933: a new perspective on the Einstein–De Sitter model of the cosmos | arxiv = 1503.08029 | journal = Eur. Phys. J. | volume = 40 | issue = 3| pages = 63–85 | doi=10.1140/epjh/e2015-50061-y| bibcode = 2015EPJH...40..301O | s2cid = 67804652 }}</ref>

The Einstein–de Sitter universe was particularly popular in the 1980s, after the theory of [[cosmic inflation]] predicted that the curvature of the universe should be very close to zero. This case with zero [[cosmological constant]] implies the Einstein–de Sitter model, and the theory of [[cold dark matter]] was developed, initially with a cosmic matter budget around 95% cold dark matter and 5% baryons. However, in the 1990s various observations including galaxy clustering and measurements of the [[Hubble constant]] led to increasingly serious problems for this model. Following the discovery of the [[accelerating universe]] in 1998, and observations of the [[cosmic microwave background]] and galaxy [[redshift survey]]s in 2000–2003, it is now generally accepted that [[dark energy]] makes up around 70 percent of the present energy density while [[cold dark matter]] contributes around 25 percent, as in the modern [[Lambda-CDM model]].

The Einstein–de Sitter model remains a good approximation to our universe in the past at redshifts between around 300 and 2, i.e. well after the radiation-dominated era but before dark energy became important.
